text.p: Seven women on Sunday became the first female graduates of the once male-dominated Philippine Military Academy (PMA), ending nearly a century of tradition.

"I say to my fellow men Filipinos, better watch out," President Fidel Ramos said in a speech, referring to the first women cadets to graduate in the 92-year history of an academy known as a male bastion.

Cheers erupted from the crowd at the PMA parade field when Ramos handed out awards to Leah Lorenzo, the 23-year-old daughter of a former Manila policeman, for finishing third with honours among 123 graduating cadets.
The seven, three of whom were placed in the top 10 of this year's graduating class, were among 16 women who enlisted for a four-year course at the academy in 1993.

A law declaring women should be treated as "equal partners" in development and nation-building cleared the way for their entry to the country's premier military school which has produced bemedalled combat officers, coup plotters and communist rebels.
Most of the leaders of six failed coup attempts from 1986 to 1989 against then president Corazon Aquino were PMA cadets who went on to become army officers.
At least two PMA cadets in the 1970s abandoned the academy to lead communist rebels against the forces of then-president Ferdinand Marcos.
On parade in blistering heat in front of Ramos, senior officials and foreign diplomats, the women were virtually indistinguishable from their male counterparts in their grey jackets and white pants.
One of them was Consuelo Nunag, who graduated in seventh position, a daughter of a mechanical engineer who himself had unsuccessfully tried to join the PMA in his youth.
The new graduates are automatically commissioned into the armed forces as lieutenants. Some of the women said they would enlist in the army, while one said she would join the air force.
Victoria Blancaflor, in her early 20s, brushed aside suggestions that women in the military should not be given combat assignments and be confined to support operations.
"If we won't be given those combat assignments we won't be promoted as aggressively as our male counterparts," she told reporters.
However, she said she believed the army would provide good opportunities for women. "I am very positive that we will be given a chance," she said.
